  • which of the five standard distributions a laboratory column plausibly follows, and how the index of dispersion tests a Poisson assumption (0.24 for hydrogen bonds, 2.88 for burst-like excursions);
  • why potencies are averaged on the pActivity scale, and that the mean pIC50 is the logarithm of the geometric mean IC50;
  • what the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem each promise, and that the CLT describes the mean and not the data;
  • how to compute a parametric interval with qt() or t.test(), check its coverage by simulation, and why a nominal 95 % interval covered only 57 % of the time on the raw concentration scale;
  • how to bootstrap any statistic with boot(), percentile versus BCa, and the three situations in which the bootstrap breaks;
  • the breakdown points of the mean, trimmed mean and median, and when robustness is worth its cost;
  • the difference between Pearson, Spearman and Kendall correlation, and why a coefficient without an interval is not evidence;
  • how to estimate the noise floor of a bioactivity dataset (0.41 log units here) and what ceiling it places on any model’s R² (0.87);
  • why 500 molecular-dynamics frames were worth 28 independent samples, and why the replica-level error bar was 26 times the naive one.

15. Self-assessment

  1. A colleague reports “mean IC50 = 4.2 µM” for a series whose median is 367 nM. What went wrong, and what should be reported instead?
The arithmetic mean was computed on the concentration scale, where a handful of very weak compounds dominate the sum; in this dataset the weakest one per cent of the compounds contribute 25.4 % of the total. Report the median IC50, or equivalently the mean pActivity back-converted (the geometric mean, 311 nM here), together with an interval.
  1. Why is the standard deviation of the data not an error bar for the mean?
Because they describe different things: the SD describes how spread out the individual observations are and does not shrink as more data are collected, while the standard error describes how precisely the mean is known and shrinks as σ/√n. Confusing them is the most common error-bar mistake in biology figures.
  1. Your 95 % confidence interval for a mean is [6.2, 6.8]. Is there a 95 % probability that the true mean lies in it?
Not under the frequentist definition. The interval either contains the true value or it does not; the 95 % refers to the long-run performance of the procedure. That probability statement belongs to a Bayesian credible interval, which Unit 10 constructs.
  1. You bootstrap the median of 8 measurements and get a very narrow interval. Should you trust it?
No. With eight points the bootstrap can only recombine eight observed values, so the replicate distribution is coarse and can be artificially tight — the series-2 histogram in Figure 8 already shows visible granularity with 59 values. Report the raw values, or use a parametric interval if the distributional assumption is defensible.
  1. The index of dispersion of a count column is 3.5. What does that tell you?
That the counts are over-dispersed relative to Poisson, usually because the underlying rate varies between units (different cells, different genes, different frames) or because events arrive in bursts, as the cage-distance excursions do at 2.88. A negative binomial model, a quasi-Poisson correction or a resampling approach is appropriate; a Poisson-based interval would be far too narrow.
  1. Your model achieves a cross-validated RMSE of 0.25 log units on this dataset. What is your first reaction?
Suspicion, not celebration. The pooled replicate standard deviation of the labels is 0.406 log units, so a model apparently more accurate than the measurements themselves almost certainly has leakage — duplicate structures across folds, a descriptor computed from the target, or a test set containing near-twins of training compounds. Check the split before anything else.
  1. Why is the Spearman correlation of −0.055 between cLogP and pActivity “significant” at p = 0.004?
Because with 2,764 compounds the standard error of the coefficient is about 0.019, so even a trivially small association is a few standard errors from zero. The p-value answers “is it exactly zero?”, which is almost never the question; the confidence interval, −0.091 to −0.017, answers “how big could it be?” and shows that the answer is “not big enough to matter”.
  1. A 1 ns trajectory saved every 2 ps gives 500 frames. How many independent measurements of the RMSD is that?
Roughly 1000 ps / (2 τ_int). With the estimator used here, τ_int for the six runs lies between about 18 and 80 ps, giving between 6 and 28 effectively independent samples per run. Any standard error computed as σ/√500 is too small by a factor of four to nine. Note that the value depends on how the autocorrelation sum is truncated, so quote the estimator along with the number.
  1. When is the percentile bootstrap interval not good enough?
When the estimator is biased, or its sampling distribution is skewed, or its variance depends on the parameter value — for example a variance ratio, an enrichment factor or a small-sample correlation. BCa corrects for the bias (z0) and the skewness (a) and should be the default for anything other than a mean; the cost is the jackknife loop, which is negligible for samples of a few thousand. In R it is one extra word: boot.ci(b, type = “bca”).
  1. Two laboratories report IC50 values of 20 nM and 200 nM for the same compound. Is one of them wrong?
Not necessarily. A one-log-unit disagreement is inside the tail of what public bioactivity data routinely show — this dataset contains sixty compounds with a range above one log unit, and the largest range is 3.30. Different assay formats, ATP concentrations and read-outs shift IC50 values systematically. Record both, flag the compound, and do not let it drive a model.
  1. Why does the mean of the pIC50 values equal the logarithm of the geometric mean of the IC50 values?
Because the logarithm turns products into sums: mean(log x) = (1/n) Σ log x_i = log((Π x_i)^(1/n)). Averaging on the log scale is averaging the exponents, which is the geometric mean on the original scale. The worked example in §4 shows both routes giving 21.87 nM, and the stopifnot in that chunk enforces it.
  1. You must report “the RMSD at 340 K” from three replicas. What do you write?
The mean of the three replica means with its standard error over n = 3 — here 0.1533 ± 0.0195 nm — stating explicitly that the interval reflects between-replica variability at 1 ns, together with the three individual run means (0.1211, 0.1884, 0.1504 nm) so the reader can see the spread. Never the frame-level standard error, and never a single replica.

Glossary

Autocorrelation time (τint)
Integral of the autocorrelation function of a time series; two successive samples separated by less than τint carry essentially the same information.
BCa interval
Bias-corrected and accelerated bootstrap interval; adjusts the percentiles for the bias and skewness of the bootstrap distribution. boot.ci(type = “bca”).
Block bootstrap
Resampling consecutive blocks of a time series instead of single observations, so that short-range dependence survives; tsboot() in the boot package.
Bootstrap
Resampling the observed data with replacement to approximate the sampling distribution of any statistic.
Breakdown point
The fraction of observations that must be corrupted before an estimator can be made arbitrarily wrong; 0 for the mean, 0.5 for the median.
Central limit theorem
The sampling distribution of a mean of independent draws with finite variance tends to a normal distribution as n grows.
Confidence interval
An interval produced by a procedure that, over repeated experiments, contains the true parameter a stated proportion of the time.
Effective sample size
The number of independent observations a correlated sample is worth, approximately n Δt / (2 τint) for a time series.
Estimator / estimate
The rule for computing a quantity from data / the number that rule returns on a particular sample.
Geometric mean
The n-th root of the product of n positive values; equals the back-transformed mean of the logarithms.
Index of dispersion
Variance divided by mean; equals 1 for a Poisson variable, below 1 for constrained counts and above 1 for over-dispersed ones.
MAD
Median absolute deviation; multiplied by 1.4826 (R’s mad() default) it estimates the standard deviation of normal data with a breakdown point of 0.5.
Noise floor
The reproducibility limit of the measurements themselves; the smallest error any model can achieve against those labels.
pActivity (pIC50)
−log10 of a potency expressed in molar units; the scale on which potencies are averaged and modelled.
Pseudoreplication
Treating repeated measurements of one experimental unit as independent replicates, which inflates the apparent sample size.
QQ-plot
Plot of sample quantiles against the quantiles of a reference distribution; straight means “same shape”. qqnorm() plus qqline() in R.
Replica
An independent repetition of a simulation with a different random seed; the experimental unit of a molecular-dynamics study.
Standard error
The standard deviation of an estimator’s sampling distribution; σ/√n for a mean of independent draws.
